claims.text: Additive manufacturing and sputtering promote microstructural refinement in high-entropy alloys relative to conventional heat treatment.
These alternative processing routes produce finer grains.
A higher density of grain boundaries impedes dislocation motion.
Restricting dislocation motion through grain refinement enhances hardness through a Hall–Petch-type effect.
Restricting dislocation motion through grain refinement enhances tensile strength through a Hall–Petch-type effect.
At fixed composition, additive-manufactured or sputtered samples will have statistically significantly smaller grains than conventionally heat-treated samples.
At fixed composition, additive-manufactured or sputtered samples will have statistically significantly greater hardness than conventionally heat-treated samples.
At fixed composition, additive-manufactured or sputtered samples will have statistically significantly greater tensile strength than conventionally heat-treated samples.
The proposed relationship is limited to conditions without deleterious phase formation, extreme residual stress, or a change into a new phase regime.
Residual stress and secondary-phase formation are potential confounding factors in attributing hardness and strength changes to grain refinement.
